newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to ease fungus limit in grain imports.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to ease fungus limit in grain imports.

text.p: Turkey will further ease its limits on the amount of fungus disease permitted in imports of some grains, a senior agriculture official said on Friday.
"The new limit will be 0.05 percent for wheat, barley and rye imports. We are working to finish the new regulation by Monday hopefully.," the official told Reuters.
Trade sources said the new limit was apparently aimed at ending controversy over grain imports from Turkey's chief ally, the United States.

Millers, U.S. farm officials and traders say the new Turkish limit would still be too stringent and would make it difficult for Turkey to moderate rises in local wheat prices, which have pushed up bread prices by 30 percent in the past two weeks.

The allowable limit was eased to 0.02 percent this week from a zero-tolerance level after criticism from U.S. officials, traders and millers. The revision came a day after the United States stopped issuing certificates for all grain exports to Turkey.
The row broke out two weeks ago when Turkey began requiring a zero-tolerance level for ergot fungus in imported wheat.

Turkish millers and traders were concerned that they might lose the United States as a major grain supplier after Ankara's crackdown on U.S. wheat imports and the ensuing U.S. ban on grains shipments.
"How will we be able to get good wheat with strict regulations like that, which you cannot find anywhere else in the world?" asked an angry miller, who declined to be named.
"The government should be logical and should not seek unrealistic standards for what it imports," he said.
The United States is a main supplier of grain for Turkey, accounting for about half of all wheat imports. Total imports this year are expected to surpass two million tonnes.

But two weeks ago Turkey held up three cargoes of U.S. milling wheat, saying they were being inspected for ergot fungus, which in large quantities can be toxic to man and animals but occurs naturally in a wide range of cereal products.

Turkey was then enforcing a zero-tolerance limit for ergot fungus in its Food Quarantine Act, but backed down this week by raising the limit to 0.02 percent after criticism from U.S. officials and from domestic traders and millers who depend on imported higher-quality wheat for flour production.

The U.S. Agriculture Department, which suspended export certificates for wheat sales to Turkey two weeks ago in response to the new policy, said on Thursday it had stopped issuing certificates for all grain and oilseed exports.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said he would meet Turkey's ambassador on Friday to discuss the issue.
Traders and farm experts say it is almost impossible to guarantee complete absence of the fungus.

"The wheat produced in Turkey also contains ergot, and in most places at levels not acceptable by the Turkish quarantine rule itself," said Ilker Tanik, secretary-general of the Turkish Millers' Association.
Millers and traders said Turkey's plans to import up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat to curb the rise in bread prices would also fall under the harsh scrutiny of the import restrictions.
